f.p: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios
f.t: Peru's Ministry of Culture has registered five interpreters and translators of the Achuar language.

f.p: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios
f.t: In Peru's 2017 national census, 6,444 people identified as part of the Achuar people.

f.p: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios
f.t: Achuar is a cross-border language, spoken in both Peru and Ecuador.

n.l: Northern Loreto in Peru near the Ecuador border, and the neighboring Amazon of Ecuador

f.t: Ashaninka of the Amônia river created their own association, Apiwtxa, in 1991; it was officially registered in 1993.
Ashenĩka, the people's own name, can be translated as my relatives, my folk or my people.
The Ashaninka of the Amônia river began an ambitious policy to protect and restore the environment of their territory.

n.l: Upper Juruá region of Acre, Brazil, including the Amônia, Breu and Envira rivers, near the Peruvian border

f.p: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios
f.t: In Peru's 2017 national census, 55,493 people identified as part of the Asháninka people.

f.p: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios
f.t: In 2017, 73,567 people in Peru said Ashaninka was the language they learned to speak as children.

n.l: Central Peruvian Amazon in Junín, Ucayali, Pasco, Cusco, Huánuco and Ayacucho

f.t: The Xavante numbered about 22,256 people in 2020.
The A'uwe (Xavante) language belongs to the Jê family of the Macro-Jê language stock.

n.l: Eastern Mato Grosso, Brazil, in Indigenous lands such as Pimentel Barbosa, Marãiwatsédé, São Marcos and Sangradouro

f.t: The Avá Guarani, called Ñandeva in Brazil, have a present-day territory that takes in parts of Mato Grosso do Sul and Paraná.
Guarani peoples, the Avá Guarani among them, live across a territory that spans regions of Brazil, Bolivia, Paraguay and Argentina.

n.l: Mato Grosso do Sul and Paraná in Brazil, and eastern Paraguay

f.p: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios
f.t: In Peru's 2017 national census, 37,693 people identified as part of the Awajún people.

f.p: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios
f.t: The Federation of Aguaruna Women of the Upper Marañón (FEMAAM), founded in Imaza in 2002, opened the way for Awajún women's political participation.

f.p: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios
f.t: The Awajún language belongs to the Jivaroan language family.

n.l: Northern Peruvian Amazon in Amazonas, Loreto, San Martín, Cajamarca and Ucayali

f.t: The Baniwa speak languages of the Arawak family along the Içana river.
Baniwa artisans are known for basketry woven from arumã fiber and are today the main producers of urutu and balaio baskets for sale.
Baniwa communities live where Brazil meets Colombia and Venezuela, along the Içana river in the Upper Rio Negro region.

n.l: Içana river and the Upper Rio Negro in Amazonas, Brazil, and neighboring Colombia and Venezuela

f.t: Guarani communities today call the places they live tekoha, a word that joins land, forest, fields, water, animals, plants and medicines.
Kaiowá, Ñandeva and Mbya Guarani all speak dialects of Guarani and show strong energy in keeping their language alive.

n.l: Southern Mato Grosso do Sul, Brazil, and neighboring eastern Paraguay, where the people are known as Paĩ Tavyterã

f.t: The Comissão Guarani Yvyrupa, founded in 2006, brings together Guarani collectives in six states of southern and southeastern Brazil.
In Guarani, yvyrupa names the structure that holds up the land, recalling free movement across territory before today's borders.
Mbya Guarani keep their language fully alive, and oral transmission is the most effective way they educate their children.

n.l: Villages across southern and southeastern Brazil, eastern Paraguay, Misiones province in Argentina, and near Montevideo in Uruguay

f.t: MAHKU, the Huni Kuin Artists Movement founded in Acre in 2013, painted a large mural across the facade of the Central Pavilion at the 2024 Venice Biennale.
Kene Kuin, meaning true design, is a pattern art that stands as an important mark of Huni Kuin identity.
Huni kuin, the name the people use for themselves, means true people, or people with known customs.

n.l: Rivers of Acre state in western Brazil, such as the Tarauacá, Jordão and Purus, and the Purus and Curanja rivers in Peru

f.t: Ka'apor communities have had a shared, standard sign language for communicating with deaf members of the community.
Ka'apor is a language of the Tupi-Guarani family.
Ka'apor featherwork is their most celebrated art, and two whole books have been devoted to it.

n.l: Northern Maranhão, Brazil, in the Alto Turiaçu Indigenous Land

f.t: About 1,500 Kichwa people of Sarayaku live in seven community centers across roughly 135,000 hectares on the Bobonaza river in Pastaza, Ecuador.
Sarayaku has its own statute on image, communication and digital sovereignty, setting free, prior and informed consent rules for visitors, press and researchers.
Sarayaku's Kawsak Sacha (Living Forest) proposal seeks legal recognition of the living forest as a new category of protected land.

n.l: Middle Bobonaza river basin, Pastaza province, Ecuadorian Amazon

f.t: Kuikuro is a southern Carib language.
Kuikuro remains a living, intact language, used by everyone in all domains except talking with outsiders.
The Kuikuro take part in the multilingual Upper Xingu system shared with neighboring peoples.

n.l: Upper Xingu, in the Xingu Indigenous Territory, Mato Grosso, Brazil

f.t: The Conselho Indígena de Roraima, founded in 1990, unites ten peoples including the Macuxi and Wapichana, with 270 of the state's 465 communities as members.
Raposa Serra do Sol Indigenous Land, 1,747,460 hectares, was ratified in April 2005, and Brazil's Supreme Court confirmed the ratification in 2009.
The Macuxi language belongs to the Carib language family.

n.l: Fields and mountains of northern Roraima, Brazil, between the headwaters of the Branco and Rupununi rivers, extending into Guyana and Venezuela

f.t: The Associação Floresta Protegida, created in 1998 by Mẽbêngôkre leaders, represents about 3,000 people in 31 villages across three Indigenous lands.
Mẽbêngôkre-Kayapó lands in Brazil cover an area of about 11 million hectares, according to the Associação Floresta Protegida.
The Mẽbêngôkre language belongs to the Jê family of the Macro-Jê language stock.

n.l: Forests and savannas of southern Pará and northern Mato Grosso, Brazil, along rivers of the Xingu basin such as the Iriri, Bacajá and Fresco

f.p: Instituto Humanitas Unisinos (republishing Conselho Indigenista Missionário)
f.t: In September 2024 Brazil's Justice Minister signed the declaration of the Sawré Muybu Indigenous Land, 178,173 hectares along the Tapajós river in Pará.
Munduruku of the upper Tapajós created the Pusuru Indigenous Association in 1991 as a formal way to organize their communities.
The Munduruku language belongs to its own Munduruku family within the Tupi language stock.

n.l: Tapajós river basin in Pará, with communities in Amazonas and Mato Grosso, Brazil

f.t: A group of Pataxó researchers has been studying their language since 1998.
Pataxó villages are spread across the far south of Bahia and the north of Minas Gerais.
The Pataxó are rebuilding their language, Patxohã, through a major community effort.

n.l: Villages in the far south of Bahia and the north of Minas Gerais, Brazil

f.p: Unidiversidad, Universidad Nacional de Cuyo (from Télam)
f.t: The Qom language is being recovered in universities and in community-run spaces, and children and teenagers are taking it up.

f.p: L'aménagement linguistique dans le monde, Université Laval (CEFAN)
f.t: Qom is one of three Indigenous languages that Argentina's Chaco province declared official alongside Spanish in 2010.

n.l: Gran Chaco of northern Argentina, especially Chaco, Formosa and Santa Fe provinces, plus communities in Buenos Aires and in Paraguay

f.t: UNESCO inscribed the oral heritage and cultural expressions of the Sápara people of Ecuador and Peru on its Representative List in 2008.
Sápara knowledge of the forest shows in their rich vocabulary for plants and animals and in their knowledge of the forest's medicinal plants.
The Sápara live in a part of the Amazon rainforest that straddles Ecuador and Peru.

n.l: Rainforest of Pastaza province in the Ecuadorian Amazon, straddling the border with Peru

f.p: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios
f.t: In Peru's 2017 national census, 25,232 people identified as part of the Shipibo-Konibo people.

f.p: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios
f.t: Peru declared kené, the Shipibo-Konibo system of geometric designs, part of the Cultural Heritage of the Nation in 2008.

f.p: Ministerio de Cultura del Perú, Base de Datos de Pueblos Indígenas u Originarios
f.t: Cantagallo, home to Shipibo-Konibo families, is the best known Amazonian Indigenous settlement in metropolitan Lima.

n.l: Ucayali, Madre de Dios, Loreto and Huánuco in Peru, with an urban community at Cantagallo in Lima

f.p: ReVista, Harvard Review of Latin America (David Rockefeller Center for Latin American Studies)
f.t: In 2022 the Shuar Aratsim Center approved its own Life Plan after participatory community workshops.

f.p: ReVista, Harvard Review of Latin America (David Rockefeller Center for Latin American Studies)
f.t: The Interprovincial Federation of Shuar Centers (FICSH), founded in 1964, was one of the pioneering Indigenous organizations of the Amazon.

f.p: ReVista, Harvard Review of Latin America (David Rockefeller Center for Latin American Studies)
f.t: Shuar territory spans the Ecuadorian provinces of Zamora Chinchipe, Morona Santiago and southern Pastaza.

n.l: Zamora Chinchipe, Morona Santiago and southern Pastaza provinces in the Ecuadorian Amazon

f.t: Farming remains the main productive activity in Terena reserves.
Terena, a language of the Arawak family, is spoken by most Terena people.
Terena people living in cities are concentrated mainly in Campo Grande, and most of them keep strong ties with their reserves.

n.l: Mato Grosso do Sul, with communities in Mato Grosso and São Paulo, Brazil

f.t: The General Organization of Bilingual Tikuna Teachers (OGPTB), created in December 1986, develops bilingual Tikuna and Portuguese education and teacher training.
Tikuna is a tonal language, considered genetically isolated, with a complex sound system and grammar.
Tikuna communities are spread across three countries: Brazil, Peru and Colombia.

n.l: Along the upper Solimões (Amazon) river in Amazonas, Brazil, and in neighboring Peru and Colombia

f.p: Institut für Archäologie und Kulturanthropologie, Universität Bonn
f.t: The Tsimane' people hold two Indigenous territories titled by the Bolivian state.

f.p: Culture and the Mind project, University of Sheffield
f.t: Almost all Tsimane' speak their own Tsimane' language as their main language.

f.p: Culture and the Mind project, University of Sheffield
f.t: Tsimane' livelihoods center on small farms of plantains, rice, corn and sweet manioc, along with fishing, hunting and gathering.

n.l: Forests and savannas of the Beni department, Bolivia, mainly along the Maniquí and Apere rivers

f.t: In 2001 Funai, Brazil's Indigenous affairs agency, officially recognized the Tupinambá of Olivença as an Indigenous people.
The Tupinambá of Olivença live in the Atlantic Forest region of southern Bahia.

n.l: Atlantic Forest of southern Bahia around Olivença, in Ilhéus, Buerarema and Una, with Tupinambá communities also in Pará, Brazil

f.t: Ecuador recognizes 679,220 hectares as belonging to the Waorani, within an ancestral territory of about 2 million hectares.
The legally recognized Waorani territory is governed by NAWE, the Waorani Nationality of Ecuador, regarded as the highest Waorani territorial authority.
Waorani territory includes 32 communities in three Amazonian provinces of Ecuador: Orellana, Pastaza and Napo.

n.l: Orellana, Pastaza and Napo provinces in the Ecuadorian Amazon

f.t: In 2012 Wapichan leaders in Guyana presented a community map and land plan titled Thinking Together for those Coming Behind Us.
The Wapichana language is classified in the Arawak language family.
Wapichana lands lie between the Branco and Rupununi rivers, on the border between Brazil and Guyana.

n.l: Northeastern Roraima, Brazil, and the South Rupununi in southwestern Guyana

f.p: L'aménagement linguistique dans le monde, Université Laval (CEFAN)
f.t: In 2010 Argentina's Chaco province made the Wichí, Qom and Moqoit languages official languages of the province alongside Spanish.

n.l: Gran Chaco of northern Argentina, mainly Salta, Formosa and Chaco provinces, with related communities in southern Bolivia

f.p: Casa Civil da Presidência da República, Governo do Brasil
f.t: About 31,000 people live in the Yanomami Indigenous Territory in Brazil, in roughly 384 villages of the Yanomami and Ye'kwana peoples.

f.p: Casa Civil da Presidência da República, Governo do Brasil
f.t: The Yanomami language family is not linked to any other language stock, and it has six languages and sixteen dialects.
The Yanomami Indigenous Territory in Brazil, about 9.66 million hectares of tropical forest, was ratified by presidential decree on 25 May 1992.

n.l: Forests of Amazonas and Roraima states in northern Brazil, continuing across the border into southern Venezuela
